London, Richard Bentley, 1834. First edition. Bennett’s first visits to Australia were in 1829 and 1832. Arriving on this second visit in springtime he became entranced with the beauty of the Australian flora. He travelled into the interior where he collected many specimens of extant and fossil fauna for Richard Owen and where his own work, especially on the platypus, had notable results. After returning to England and publishing this book, Bennett, who was a medical practitioner, returned to settle permanently in Sydney in 1836. Here he established a successful practice and became arguably the leading contemporary figure in colonial science. Abbey, 527; Ferguson, 1743; Whittell, 49. Estimate $500/700

title: DARLING, Lieutenant-General Ralph, Governor.
description: DARLING, Lieutenant-General Ralph, Governor. NEW SOUTH WALES. PAPERS EXPLANATORY OF THE CHARGES brought against Lieut. Gen. Darling, by William Charles Wentworth, Esq. Foolscap folio, sewn, housed in modern folding cloth-backed papered boards portfolio with ribbon ties. London, Ordered, by The House of Commons, to be Printed, 1 July 1830. Following the agitation of opposition Members of Parliament, the Colonial Secretary published these dispatches from New South Wales. The tabling of these papers was a thoroughly dishonest representation of the Wentworth – Darling affair, anticipating, without ambiguity, the way the government would handle the whole matter. Darling’s dispatches relating to Wentworth’s attempted impeachment of him with all the various attachments and enclosures were printed here “exclusive of a Letter, also therein enclosed, addressed by Mr. William Charles Wentworth to the Right Honourable Sir George Murray…”. In other words, Darling’s defence against Wentworth’s charges, the Executive Council’s detailed critical response to Wentworth’s letter of impeachment, and other supporting documents were laid upon the table and printed but not the very case for impeachment that formed the crux of the entire affair! Once this deceptive conduct was revealed by Robison and his allies in the famous pamphlet by “Miles”, the Colonial Office was forced to reveal the entire text of the Wentworth impeachment and it was published in the Parliamentary Papers in 1832. Ferguson, 1355. Estimate $400/600

title: EDEN, William (traditional misattribution).
description: EDEN, William (traditional misattribution). THE HISTORY OF NEW HOLLAND, from its First Discovery in 1616, to the Present Time. With a Particular Account of its Produce and Inhabitants; and a Description of Botany Bay: also, A List of the Naval, Marine, Military, and Civil Establishment. To which is prefixed, An Introductory Discourse on Banishment, by the Right Honourable William Eden. Octavo, two engraved folding maps handcoloured in outline, with an advertisement leaf (not noted by Ferguson), pale stain at foot several leaves, uncut, later half roan and boards. London, Printed for John Stockdale, 1787. Second edition. This important First Fleet book, one of the earliest descriptions of Australia, was written when the expedition to settle New Holland was first proposed publicly in 1786-7. The prominent Piccadilly bookseller and publisher, John Stockdale, published the work aiming “to present at one view a connected description of the whole country of New Holland” to a public anxious for information on Botany Bay and the proposed thief colony there. The preface and text discuss the transportation of offenders, with an “Introductory Discourse on Banishment” by William Eden, to whom authorship of the whole book was for a long time attributed. Details of the fleet that was preparing to depart are given as well as a comprehensive account of what was known of the east coast of New Holland. The two fine handcoloured maps are highly regarded and show the entire continent as then known, with an inset map of Botany Bay, and a large folding world map with the “passage from England to Botany Bay in New Holland 1787” showing the route of the First Fleet. Stockdale was exceptionally well-connected in official circles and this and other works that he published in 1786-7 relating to the proposed Botany Bay experiment were almost certainly prepared with official approval. These livres de circonstance, as Eris O’Brien called them, were essentially part of a publicity campaign by the proBotany-Bay lobby within Whitehall circles. Beddie, 27; Davidson, pp. 79–81 (“an extremely interesting work and an essential inclusion in all comprehensive collections”); Ferguson, 24; Holmes, 66. Estimate $2000/3000 Lot 18

title: GURNER, Henry Field. A SIGNIFICANT ARCHIVE relating to Henry Field Gurner as author, historian, and book collector.
description: GURNER, Henry Field. A SIGNIFICANT ARCHIVE relating to Henry Field Gurner as author, historian, and book collector. Born in 1819 in Sydney, Henry Field Gurner was the son of John Gurner, clerk to Judge Barron Field in the Supreme Court of New South Wales. His own legal career began in 1834, and in 1841 he accompanied Judge Willis to Port Phillip as Deputy-Registrar and Clerk of the Supreme Court. Within a decade Gurner was appointed Crown Solicitor of the Colony, a position which he held for thirty years. Gurner was an early member of the Melbourne Club, joining in 1844, and serving as President in 1870. In 1851 he married Augusta Curr, daughter of Edward Curr, Tasmanian and Victorian pastoralist, and author of Account of the Colony of Van Diemen’s Land. Her brother was E.M. Curr, whose Recollections of Squatting in Victoria was published in 1883. Gurner’s Chronicle of Port Phillip... from 1770 to 1840, was published in 1876. The author’s own copy, present here, has been extended from its 52-pages by over 400 pages of his closely written manuscript notes, half of which continue the history from the end of 1839 until late in the year 1851. Also present in the archive is a substantial bound manuscript volume of biographical summaries of (mainly) early Sydney convicts and colonists, and a bound ledger of chronological historical notes. Gurner was an enthusiastic book collector and his activities are documented in his own copy of his 1878 library catalogue, Books on the Colonies and Colonial Publications in possession of Henry Field Gurner, Melbourne. This is signed by him, retaining the original front wrapper, in a ticketed Pownceby binding, with price information and interleaved additions. Also bound in is his subsequent Publications on the Colonies, Wanted by H.F.G., August 1880, with further printed lists of Pamphlets. A second copy of the catalogue is inscribed by Henry to his son Henry E. Gurner in October 1878. Two further copies of the Publications Wanted, each with markings and annotations, are present. The archive includes two autograph letters from E.M. Curr to his nephew Henry E. Gurner in 1884, following Henry F. Gurner’s death, in which Curr explains his own role in working on Gurner’s catalogue, and gives financial details on the publication of his own Recollections (also included are some family manuscripts poems of 1870s, of social interest and with references to Geelong, squatting &c.). Henry’s father, John (1792-1882), noted by Charles Stitz as possibly the earliest serious book collector in the colony, had arrived in Sydney in 1817, and worked as Chief Clerk of the Supreme Court under Barron Field. Father and son died only a year apart, in 1882 and 1883 respectively, and there is little record of what became of their libraries, beyond the Sydney catalogue of John Gurner’s law books (see below), and a letter between two of Henry’s sons (still retained in the family) noting the sale in 1884 of Henry’s Argus, Leader, and other newspapers to the Public Library of Victoria, for an amount of £75. In detail the archive comprises: (1) Chronicle of Port Phillip ... from 1770 to 1840 (Melbourne, 1876), the author’s copy with extensive annotation and additional leaves of manuscript text, with pencilled inscription from H.F.G. to Hy E. Gurner, used original printed wrappers with worn reinforced backstrip. + A second copy in original wrappers, initialled on the front wrapper “H.F.Gs copy”, with several manuscript additions and amendments, and a third copy in original wrappers, inscribed to H.E. Gurner from “H.F.G.” (2) Books on the Colonies and Colonial Publications in possession of Henry Field Gurner, Melbourne, Victoria 1878 [bound with] Publications on the Colonies, Wanted by H.F.G., August 1880, signed by the author, with a manuscript index, price information and interleaved additions, retaining the original front wrapper, in a ticketed Pownceby binding of half roan (backstrip split at joint and lacking the lower third of backstrip). + Henry E. Gurner’s copy of the catalogue, signed by him, with original front wrapper, in early semi-limp morocco. (3) 1882 Catalogue, of twenty numbered leaves printed on rectos only, without imprint, interleaved and annotated, in contemporary cloth, gilt title to spine. (4) Publications on the Colonies, Wanted by H.F.G. 1880. H.E. Gurner’s copy, signed, with extensive manuscript annotations including on several loosely inserted sheets. + Two further copies, each with manuscript notes and amendments. (5) Octavo ledger, manuscript biographical summaries with index, on 138 numbered pages, original half roan, lower backstrip detached. (6) Foolscap folio ledger, manuscript historical notes on 44 pages, plus blanks, original half roan (chipped) and marbled boards. (7) Foolscap folio ledger, manuscript alphabetical catalogue on 341 pages, original half reversed calf with leather labels on front board and spine. (8) Two a.l.s. from Edward M. Curr, St. Kilda, 22 August 1883, 4 pages, and 17 April 1884, 8 pages. + Henry E. Gurner manuscript copy of letter to E.M. Curr, 13 March 1884, 4 pages. (9) Series of manuscript poems, apparently from members of the Curr family, unsigned, one dated June 1857, another October 1876, with references to St Kilda, Geelong, Collingwood. With 2 printed family death notices. (10) Catalogue of Law Books belonging to the Estate of the late John Gurner, Esq., Solicitor, to be sold by Auction by H. Vaughan, at his rooms, 142 King Street East on Wednesday, Aug. 9, 1882 (wrapper title). Octavo, original printed wrappers. Sydney, F. White (Printer), 1882. 164 lots in all, with loosely inserted manuscript results and accounting. (11) Engraved armorial bookplate of Henry Field Gurner. Estimate $5000/8000

title: HARRIS, Alexander. SETTLERS AND CONVICTS; or, Recollections of Sixteen Years’ Labour in the Australian Backwoods.
description: HARRIS, Alexander. SETTLERS AND CONVICTS; or, Recollections of Sixteen Years’ Labour in the Australian Backwoods. By an Emigrant Mechanic. Duodecimo, a very good copy in original cloth, free front endpaper excised. London, G. Cox, 1847. First edition: one of the classic accounts of pre-gold rush Australia. Exiled by his family to New South Wales in 1825, Alexander Harris worked as a cedar getter until leaving Australia in 1841. Returning to London he became associated with the movement to promote emigration and wrote or co-wrote several works, most notably this influential account of Australian backwoods life, describing and analysing his own experiences. This is acknowledged as the most significant early articulation of the spirit of Australian egalitarianism. Ferguson, 4529. Estimate $200/300

title: LANG, John Dunmore. COOKSLAND IN NORTH-EASTERN AUSTRALIA; The future cotton-field of Great Britain: its characteristics
description: LANG, John Dunmore. COOKSLAND IN NORTH-EASTERN AUSTRALIA; The future cotton-field of Great Britain: its characteristics and capabilities for European colonization. With a disquisition on the Origin, Manners, and Customs of the Aborigines. title: LESSON, René Primevère.
description: LESSON, René Primevère. VOYAGE AUTOUR DU MONDE entrepris par ordre du Gouvernement sur la Corvette La Coquille; par P. Lesson, Membre correspondant de l’Institut. Two volumes in four, octavo (205 x 130 mm), handcoloured natural history plates, and engraved plates, intermittent pale browning, a short split in the blank margin of the frontispiece portrait, one plate with expert repairs along blank margin, in a handsome recent French binding of quarter crimson morocco, in matching slipcase edged in morocco. Paris, P. Pourrat Frères, 1839. First edition. The official account of the 1822-5 voyage in the Coquille under Louis Isidore Duperrey was never completed and so this scarce account by the surgeon and naturalist on the Coquille is the only separate narrative account. Lesson reported many important scientific details which Duperrey failed to publish in his unfinished account, including many extensive vocabularies and grammatical analyses, particularly of the Maori language. The illustrations in Lesson’s work include over twenty plates of views, native costumes, objects and tools, as well as coastal profiles, while the beautiful, delicate handcoloured plates include illustrations of the kangaroo, kiwi, lyrebird, opossum, parrots, platypus, wombat, and several Birds of Paradise. In a small number of copies the non-integral illustrated title-page of the first volume (only) has the date 1838. The work was issued in livraisons – more or less, “parts” – over 1838-9. Ferguson’s treatment of the work contains substantial errors: his 2533 (describing copies with the mixed 1838 and 1839 title-pages), for example, calls for only 37 plates, giving rise to a belief in earlier years that there were two editions of the book, with the 1839 “edition” having more plates. In addition, Ferguson initially transposed the collation of the two volumes in error (2787). Ferguson, 2787(rev); Hill 2, 1012; Hocken, p. 73; Sabin, 40214; Wantrup 2nd edition (in publication), 329. Estimate $1000/2000

title: MITCHELL, Thomas Livingstone.
description: MITCHELL, Thomas Livingstone. THREE EXPEDITIONS INTO THE INTERIOR OF EASTERN AUSTRALIA, with descriptions of the recently explored region of Australia Felix, and of the present Colony of New South Wales. Two volumes, octavo, with plates (some coloured), and coloured maps, the large folding map laid on fine linen, strictly contemporary calf, the spines with five contrasting labels – some distressed – each with the gilt ornaments repeated from the publisher’s cloth binding, marbled endpapers; with the armorial bookplate of William Bragge and the later signed Perrotet bookplate of E.E. Pescott (and with two 1940s Mitchell postal stamps laid in). London, T. & W. Boone, 1839. The revised second edition. Ferguson, 2811; Wantrup, 125. This we believe to be a hitherto unnoticed special publisher’s binding with contrasting spine labels repeating the gilt ornaments of the cloth issue. Engineer, antiquarian, book collector, bibliographer, philanthropist, and author, William Bragge, whose armorial bookplate is on the endpaper here, appears to have been the original owner. description: RUDDER, E.W. INCIDENTS CONNECTED WITH THE DISCOVERY OF GOLD in New South Wales, in the Year 1851… Being a Personal Narrative of his Connection With That Event. Octavo, original green printed wrappers with decorative border, title repeated on front wrapper (bit chipped on spine). Sydney, Frederick White, 1861. Rare: first edition. Enoch William Rudder was a crucial figure in the story of Hargraves’s discovery of payable gold in Australia. “Rudder never disputed the fact that Hargraves made known the existence of payable gold but he did claim, with slight overstatement, ‘to have laid its foundation, to have been its promulgator, and the first demonstrator of the most simple and efficient method of procuring it’. In support of his case, he published in Sydney in 1861 a short pamphlet, now quite rare... He presented a great deal of evidence in the 42 pages of his narrative without too much exaggeration... His claim was not entirely unreasonable and the justice of it was supported by the findings of an 1880 Parliamentary Select Committee. The greatest interest in Rudder’s pamphlet, however, lies not in his case but in his narrative of the events leading up to the Ophir rush that usefully supplements the accounts of Hargraves and Davison” (Wantrup). Oblong folio, letterpress title-page and five tinted lithographed plates, with leaves of letterpress description, one plate with minor marking at blank corner, several leaves with small tissue strengthening at corner tips, an attractive copy in the original wrappers, the front wrapper illustrated by six vignettes of goldfields scenes by Tulloch, loosely inserted in protective cloth covers, with contemporary Melbourne gift inscription. description: STREETON, Arthur. A SERIES OF EIGHT SPLENDID LONG AND ILLUSTRATED AUTOGRAPH LETTERS, SIGNED to the owner of his painting ‘Golden Summer’ (1888), Mrs H.R. Mackenzie. Twenty-six pages on 24 small quarto sheets, ink manuscript with ink and watercolour sketches, on printed 17 Grange Road and ‘Fairlie House’ (7 Anderson Street) letterhead, pages affixed with pins, in very good state (old folds). Melbourne, 2 & 26 April 1924, 2 & 17 May 1924, 8 & 17 April 1930; 10 December 1931; and 18 March 1937. A series of letters mostly discussing Streeton’s ‘Golden Summer’ including the delivery of the painting to the new owner on her birthday, and the reproduction of the painting in The Arthur Streeton Catalogue (1935). In the first letter (dated 2 April 1924) Streeton wrote: ‘I am delighted that ‘Golden Summer’ now belongs to you, for it belongs to the time when Conder, Roberts & I used to pawn our possessions in order to carry on & they were also our happiest days”. First sold in 1892, “Golden Summer’” was bought back by Streeton in 1919 and subsequently sold to Mrs Mackenzie for 1000 guineas. The letters includes four sketches of views from “Fairlie House” including the Botanic Gardens and Government House, Port Phillip Bay, and the You Yangs and Corio Bay. In the final letter, written after his knighthood, Streeton sketches himself under a shining crown “dazed by the Rays of Royalty”. Estimate $5000/8000
